## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Cūḷanāradajātaka* (Ja 477) is a narrative belonging to the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the traditional introductory setting recorded in the text's blurb, the Buddha delivered the story while residing at Jetavana to address the allurements of a coarse girl, opening with the verse line "No wood is chopt" [SuttaCentral]. The text is also cited in the post-canonical *Milindapañha* in the *Gharakapotaṅgapañha* (Mil 7.6.4) [SuttaCentral].
In modern scholarship, the commentary to the *Cūḷanāradajātaka* has been examined for its socio-historical terminology, specifically regarding an occurrence of the term *Sākiya-bhikkhu* in an episode where a mother attempts to entrap a monk as a husband for her daughter [Williams, Critical Concepts].
Textual parallels and reuse data from DharmaNexus identify extensive Pali-internal correspondence with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (*Catuttho bhāgo*), comprising six matching segments, the longest covering §6.1–14.4 [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also detects minor cross-language alignments with a Tibetan medical treatise, the *Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayanāmavaiḍūryakabhāṣya* (D4311), though SuttaCentral records no curated canonical parallels in other languages [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
